clue.text: Before "heavy" singer loses central mass, turn over astronomer

indicators.note: Before tells us the turn-over piece is placed ahead of the singer piece in the answer

parts.note: PTO is the familiar abbreviation for 'please turn over' at the foot of a page

indicators.note: loses central says the letter in the very middle of the singer's name drops out

parts.note: Lemmy was the frontman of the heavy metal band Motorhead
M is the standard abbreviation for mass in physics

explanation.surface: A heavy-metal vocalist slims down and then flips over to look at the stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heavy' in quotes points to heavy metal; Lemmy fronted Motorhead. 'loses central' takes out one of the two middle letters, and 'Before' puts the page instruction first.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alexandrian scholar behind the geocentric model of the heavens is the classic ancient astronomer.

clue.text: Air-raid shelter impressing oriental boss shut outside!

indicators.note: impressing is read as pressing one piece into another, so the oriental boss goes inside
outside confirms the word for shut sits round the other letters as a wrapper

parts.note: a door pushed to is shut, so 'to' can mean shut
E for east, the oriental direction
a stud is a raised boss or knob on a surface

explanation.surface: An eastern chief barricades himself in a bomb shelter and locks the door.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: the Roman legion's roof of overlapping shields protected soldiers from missiles raining down from above, a shelter from an air raid of sorts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman tortoise formation of locked shields overhead was a defence against arrows and stones falling from the sky.

clue.text: Joely Richardson's giving up the theatre

indicators.note: giving up is read as yielding a few letters from inside the actress's name

explanation.surface: An actress quits the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lyric is a well-known theatre on London's Shaftesbury Avenue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lyric is a long-standing West End playhouse, so it is a theatre by name.

clue.text: Compiler's cover for "Listener" — or I'm a Dutchman

indicators.note: for Listener means the phrase is judged by how it strikes the ear of someone hearing it

parts.note: a setter refers to self as me, so compiler's gives MINE, and hair is the cover on one's head

explanation.surface: A setter swears about a pseudonym used in the Listener crossword, using the old idiom of disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listener' looks like the name of the crossword series; it marks a sound-alike. MINE HAIR, said aloud, gives the Dutch form of address. The phrase 'or I'm a Dutchman' is an English expression of certainty.
explanation.definitionFit: Mynheer is the Dutch equivalent of 'sir' or 'Mr', used in English for a Dutch gentleman.

clue.text: Cup-carrying individual's introduction to nurse in liquor store

indicators.note: introduction to means one piece is brought into the middle of the other

parts.note: SEN is a State Enrolled Nurse, a former British nursing grade
Hebe was the cupbearer to the Greek gods; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: A carer is introduced to someone holding a cup in an off-licence.
explanation.walkthrough: A shebeen is an unlicensed drinking den, originally Irish.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebeen is an illicit bar or drinking house selling alcohol without a licence.

clue.text: Spanish chap welcoming a couple of brothers in

indicators.note: welcoming means taking a guest inside, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to be in is to be at home

indicators.note: a couple of brothers means just the first two letters of that word

explanation.surface: A Spaniard invites two siblings indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: Hombre is the Spanish word for man, used in English slang for a fellow.

clue.text: Measure from Rio, say, gives excellent analysis by statistician …

parts.note: boss is slang for excellent or first-rate
ANOVA is analysis of variance, a standard statistical technique

explanation.surface: Someone from Rio gets top marks from a number-cruncher's study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' here means a dance or rhythm, not a quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: Bossa nova is a Brazilian dance rhythm associated with Rio de Janeiro, a measure in the sense of a dance.

clue.text: … and others describing source of riches that is forbidden for ever

indicators.note: describing in its sense of drawing round means one piece encircles the other

parts.note: et al is the Latin abbreviation for and others

indicators.note: forbidden says the letters for 'that is' are not allowed in the piece

parts.note: ERNIE is the machine that draws British Premium Bond prize numbers
ie is the abbreviation for that is (id est)

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: others speak of a fortune that is banned forever.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots continue the previous clue's surface. ERNIE picks British Premium Bond prizes, a state savings lottery; 'forbidden' drops the abbreviation, and 'describing' wraps the Latin phrase round what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eternal lasts for ever, with no end, so the adjective and phrase are synonyms.

clue.text: Is this why people hang out at the Comedy Club?

definitions.text: Is this why people hang out at the Comedy Club?

parts.words: Is this why people hang out at the Comedy Club?
parts.note: hang out reads as being hanged as well as frequenting a place, so the clue asks about jokes made at the scaffold

explanation.walkthrough: 'hang out' means spending time somewhere, but also suggests the gallows.
explanation.definitionFit: Grim jokes made in the face of death or disaster are humour of the scaffold.

clue.text: Emperor gets around shaving more on the right than the left

indicators.text: shaving more on the right than the left
indicators.note: shaving trims the ends of the phrase, two letters off the left and four off the right

explanation.surface: A ruler shaves one side of his face more closely than the other.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'shaving' leaves the inside run of the two words, with more cut from the right end than the left.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsar was the emperor of Russia before the 1917 revolution.

clue.text: Tight young women — we might as well have been a mile away

definitions.text: we might as well have been a mile away

parts.note: near is an old word for tight in the sense of stingy
misses are young unmarried women

explanation.surface: Some mean girls say the attempt fell well short.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the proverb 'a miss is as good as a mile': a narrow failure is still a failure.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow failure is no better than a wide one, as the proverb about a mile says.

clue.text: Having liquorice to cook with her — an extraordinary dish!

indicators.note: to cook means the letters are worked up together into something new, as ingredients are

explanation.surface: A cook adds sweets to a recipe and produces a strange dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to cook' signals rearranging LIQUORICE, HER and AN as one pool; 'extraordinary' is the setter's praise of the dish it defines, not a second signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The French open tart of eggs, cream and bacon is a classic dish, here praised as out of the ordinary.

clue.text: See 12
Promise in future to have long boxed details of TV programme

definitions.text: Promise in future to have long boxed details of TV programme

parts.words: Promise in future to have long boxed details of TV programme
parts.note: reads as a long-running show on the box that set out the promise of what lies ahead, technology and inventions to come

explanation.surface: A broadcaster promises future details of a long-running TV show.
explanation.walkthrough: The BBC science programme ran from 1965 to 2003, showing coming inventions; 'boxed' means shown on the box (television).
explanation.definitionFit: The long-running BBC show presenting future technology took its name from the world of the coming day.

clue.text: It'll dry moist places with little adjustment at last to seal you in

indicators.note: to seal says one piece closes round the other and holds it
in completes the sealing phrase, putting the second piece inside
a little adjustment at last swaps the final two letters of the watery places

parts.note: oases are moist spots in a desert
thou is the old form of you

explanation.surface: A damp-proofing product promises to seal you in after a slight tweak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with little adjustment at last' swaps the final two letters, making OASSE, before 'to seal ... in' encloses the old word for you. An oast house is a hop-drying kiln, familiar in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: An oast house is a building with a kiln for drying hops, so it is the thing that dries.

clue.text: See 14
Harden case having got supply, inhaling H

definitions.text: Harden case having got supply, inhaling H

indicators.note: inhaling means taking a letter inside the mixed letters
supply in its sense of supple or bendable means these letters are flexible and rearranged

parts.note: H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A hardened addict has got his supply and is breathing in heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines and builds: anagram HARDEN CASE GOT, and take in H, heroin, to describe smoking heroin by inhaling its fumes.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhaling the fumes of heated heroin is the slang practice described by this phrase.

clue.text: Unbeliever put chicken in microwave?

parts.note: to microwave food is to heat it
a hen is a chicken

explanation.surface: Someone puts a chicken in the microwave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put ... in' looks like a container instruction; here the pieces simply sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen is someone who does not hold the religious faith of others, an unbeliever.

clue.text: See 17
Fool, say, with hair put up

indicators.note: put up means raised, which in a down answer reads the word from the bottom upwards

parts.note: tressed means having tresses, or hair

explanation.surface: An idiot wears his hair up.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool is a British pudding of fruit and cream, so 'Fool, say' is an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A fool is a pudding of puréed fruit folded into cream, an example of a sweet course.

clue.text: So the enemy's winning nothing — area's within limit

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

indicators.note: within means the area letter goes inside the limit word

parts.note: a verge is an edge or limit

explanation.surface: The foe is ahead with none conceded, and the area lies inside the boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The enemy' is time, as in 'time is the enemy': if time is winning, you are too old.
explanation.definitionFit: Being past the permitted age means time has got the better of you.

clue.text: Egghead's departing in vessel

indicators.note: in places the leaving word inside the container word

parts.note: a bin is a container or vessel
off means departing, leaving

explanation.surface: A clever person is leaving aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' suggests a ship, but it is a bin.
explanation.definitionFit: A boffin is British slang for a scientist or intellectual, an egghead.

clue.text: Most bachelors need a varied source of personal morning reading

indicators.note: varied means the letters are changed about into another order

explanation.surface: Bachelors need a range of morning newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reading' suggests a newspaper, but it is the number shown when you step on.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathroom scales give a private weight reading, usually taken first thing in the morning.

clue.text: See 23
Play partly over — misbehave

parts.note: an act is one part of a play
up means over or finished, as in 'time's up'

explanation.surface: The performance is half done, and someone starts behaving badly.
explanation.definitionFit: To act up is to behave badly or play up, a phrasal idiom for misbehaving.

clue.text: Use a cuff, eh? Mad, she drives me

indicators.note: mad means crazy, so the letters go wildly out of order

explanation.surface: A woman is driven crazy and asks whether to hit someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drives me' looks like 'drives me mad'; it means she is my driver.
explanation.definitionFit: A chauffeuse is a female chauffeur, a woman employed to drive someone.

clue.text: Fur supplier has head shaved precisely

indicators.note: head shaved means the first letter is cut off

parts.note: the stoat supplies ermine fur in its winter coat

explanation.surface: A furrier's animal has its head shaved neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: To a T means exactly or perfectly, an idiom for precisely.

clue.text: Suppose the answer isn't "a positive Hell"?

parts.note: to infer is to deduce or suppose
an answer that is not a positive one, not yes, is no

explanation.surface: A puzzled thinker wonders whether the answer is a definite hell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a positive Hell' looks like one phrase; the definition is just Hell.
explanation.definitionFit: Inferno is Italian for hell, and Dante's Inferno made it a byword for the underworld.

clue.text: Southern comic getting a bung

parts.note: The Topper was a British children's comic published by DC Thomson

explanation.surface: A comedian from the south receives a bribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bung' suggests a bribe but means a plug.
explanation.definitionFit: A bung is a plug or stopper for closing a hole or bottle.
